english: Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the saṃghāta (aggregate of body and senses), cetanā (awareness) and dhṛti (steadiness): these named here are the vikāra (modifications). What was listed before them, from the great elements onward, is the kṣetra (field) itself, so 'this field with its modifications, told in brief' covers both lists, the field and then what changes in it.
divergence_note: Read with Jayatīrtha's Prameyadīpikā on Madhva's bhāṣya (their 13.7): Madhva gives one sentence: desire and the rest are the vikāra (modifications). Jayatīrtha only settles its scope: after the list beginning with the great elements the verse says 'this field with its modifications', which leaves unclear what is the field and what its modifications, and Madhva's sentence answers that desire and the rest are the modifications, the implication being that the earlier list is the field. That is a clarification of how the two lists divide, not a new doctrine. Neither commentator says whose property desire is, nor how cetanā (awareness) or dhṛti (steadiness) are to be taken, so the Dvaita text here takes no side in the dispute the other schools engage: Advaita, Bhakti and Advaita-bhakti make desire and the rest properties of the mind, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Śuddhādvaita make them properties of the self that arise through its tie to the field. The Dvaita reading supplied is only that these items fall under the field as its modifications.
everyday_application: When something at work is going wrong, write two separate lists before diagnosing: the standing structure (the people, the tools, the schedule, the budget) and the shifting states running through it (enthusiasm, irritation, fatigue, a good week). Keeping them apart stops a team from treating a passing mood as a structural flaw, or a structural flaw as somebody's bad mood.
